slides.title: Fair questions first
slides.text: A survey asks people questions. The answers can only be fair if the questions are fair.
slides.alt: One plain survey question, Pets at home, tallied: Dog 12, Cat 3, Fish 4, Bird 0, Rabbit 0, None 2.

focus.cue: One plain question: pets at home
Every answer is counted the same

slides.title: Leading questions
slides.text: A question that pushes people toward one answer is a leading question. It builds bias into the data before anyone counts.
slides.alt: Pick a question: pets, colors, fruit, sport, how we get to school, or our own question.

focus.cue: Or your own question: keep it fair

slides.title: Fix the question
slides.text: Ask in a way that lets every answer feel equally welcome.
steps: leading: Don't you agree homework is too long?
fair: Is homework too long, about right or too short?

slides.title: A bigger, fairer sample
slides.text: More answers from more kinds of people make a fairer sample. Even a few missing answers can change a close result.
slides.alt: The lunch vote sorted by Voted: every No is a veggie eater. The screen stood in the meat line.

focus.cue: Every No is a veggie eater
The screen only reached the meat line

slides.title: Compare by percent
slides.text: Our class: 6 of 12 picked blue, which is 50%. The other class is a different size, so compare shares: 50% against their 33%, not 6 against their count.
slides.alt: Favorite colors in percent: ours next to another class. Blue is 50% here and 33% there.

focus.cue: Percent makes different sizes fair to compare

words.means: something that pushes results unfairly one way
a person who answers a survey
how many out of 100, for fair comparisons

slides.title: Your mission
slides.text: Open Data Detective at My Data. Chart one survey question, clean it, and compare it with another class by percent.
